mcqs.question: A service opens a brand-new TCP+TLS connection for every single database call instead of reusing one. At 1,000 requests/sec, what is the main cost of this approach?
options: Most of the server's time gets spent on connection setup (handshake, TLS, auth) rather than actual request processing
There is no meaningful cost — modern networks make connection setup effectively free
The database will reject all connections after the first one
TLS makes repeated connection setup faster than reusing an existing connection
mcqs.explanation: Handshake and TLS negotiation cost real round trips — tens of milliseconds — that can dwarf what a fast query itself takes, so paying it every request wastes most of the time budget on setup, not work. Connection setup isn't free, the database doesn't uniquely reject repeat connections, and reusing a warm connection is always cheaper than renegotiating TLS from scratch.

mcqs.question: A connection pool is configured with a maximum of 4 connections, all 4 currently checked out to in-flight requests. A 5th request arrives, and the pool has no queue timeout configured that would reject it immediately. What happens?
options: The pool creates a 5th connection immediately to serve the new request
The request waits until one of the 4 connections is returned to the pool
The request is silently dropped with no error
The pool closes one of the 4 in-flight connections to free capacity for the new request
mcqs.explanation: A pool at its configured maximum does not exceed that ceiling — it doesn't spin up an extra connection past max, silently drop requests, or forcibly cut off an in-flight connection to make room. The new request queues, waiting for one of the existing connections to be returned.

mcqs.question: A team sizes their connection pool based on 'as many connections as our service could theoretically use,' without checking what the downstream database can sustain. What is the likely outcome under load?
options: The pool will automatically shrink itself to match the database's actual capacity
Nothing — pool size on the caller side has no effect on the downstream server
The service can send more concurrent work at the database than it can handle, causing the database to degrade under the connection overhead itself
The database will silently queue excess connections with no performance impact
mcqs.explanation: Pools don't self-tune to the callee's real capacity, and pool size on the caller side directly determines how much concurrent load the callee receives — it isn't inert. Sizing from the caller's ambition rather than the callee's sustainable concurrency is exactly how a pool ends up too big, overwhelming the database's own connection overhead rather than queuing harmlessly.

mcqs.question: In the connection-pool checkout code, why does the `finally: pool.release(conn)` block matter as much as the checkout timeout?
options: It has no real effect — `finally` blocks are purely a style convention in this context
It prevents the database from ever seeing more than one connection at a time
It automatically retries the query if it fails
Without it, an exception during query execution would skip returning the connection, permanently shrinking the pool by one each time it happens
mcqs.explanation: The `finally` block guarantees the connection goes back to the pool even if the query raises an exception; skip it and every such failure leaks one connection out of the pool permanently, eventually draining it to zero. It doesn't limit the database to one connection, doesn't add retry behavior, and is functionally significant here, not merely stylistic.

mcqs.question: A service runs with a per-instance database connection pool of 20, and autoscales from 5 instances to 50 during a traffic spike. What is the most likely consequence for the database?
options: The database automatically increases its own connection limit to match demand
The database goes from seeing 100 connections to seeing up to 1,000, likely exceeding its configured connection limit and causing 'too many connections' errors fleet-wide
Nothing changes, since each instance's pool size stayed the same at 20
The extra instances will automatically share connections from the original 5 instances' pools
mcqs.explanation: The database experiences the sum of every instance's pool, not one instance's view — 50 instances at 20 connections each is 1,000, not 100 — and databases don't self-expand their connection limits or let instances share pools across process boundaries. This is exactly the pitfall: a pool size that looks modest per instance becomes dangerous multiplied across the fleet's peak size.
